title: Cheeni in Durham Named North Carolina's Best Indian Restaurant in National Ranking
excerpt: Tasting Table puts chef Preeti Waas's family-owned downtown Durham restaurant at No. 1 in the state, ahead of every other Indian kitchen in North Carolina.
body:
• Cheeni, at 202 Corcoran St Ste 100 in downtown Durham, ranks as the No. 1 Indian restaurant in North Carolina in Tasting Table's best-Indian-food-in-every-state list.
  • Chef Preeti Waas, a James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in 2023 and 2024, runs the family-owned restaurant with her daughter Amy Waas.
  • What to order: start with samosa chaat, then try the fish moilee with paratha, the paneer makhani, or the lamb vindaloo for a tour of regions across India.
  • Cheeni Durham is dinner-only, open seven days a week — Sunday to Thursday 5-9 p.m., Friday and Saturday 4-10 p.m. — and reservations are highly encouraged, especially for parties of five or more.

The best Indian food in North Carolina is served in downtown Durham, according to a new state-by-state ranking. Tasting Table named Cheeni the top Indian restaurant in North Carolina in its list of where to find the best Indian food in every state, a result first reported locally by the Raleigh News & Observer.

Tasting Table said it built the 50-state list using online customer reviews, local press and awards received by each restaurant. For North Carolina, it pointed to personal experience of the kitchen, writing that Cheeni does justice to the cuisine without adopting too many Western influences, and singling out dishes from the samosa chaat to the paneer makhani.

A homestyle kitchen with national honours

Cheeni is a family-owned restaurant led by chef Preeti Waas and her daughter Amy Waas. Waas was a James Beard Award semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in both 2023 and 2024, according to coverage of the ranking, and Tasting Table noted she often personally makes the rounds to check on diners at the downtown Durham restaurant.

The Durham restaurant opened in November 2023 and built its reputation quickly. The concept itself is older: Waas developed Cheeni from a street-style kiosk idea born of her love of baking, and the name Cheeni means sugar. The restaurant's own site describes the downtown location as a dinner-only, a la carte concept whose menu rotates semi-frequently, built around regionally inspired, sentimental dishes tied to Waas's own food memories.

What to order

The menu is deliberately regional rather than a standard North Indian takeout list. Tamil Nadu, Kerala and West Bengal all show up on one menu, alongside dishes from the Karnataka coast. The fish moilee, a Kerala coconut curry served with paratha, and the Mangalorean chicken are among the southern choices, while the lamb vindaloo carries the vinegar and dried red chilli heat of the western coast.

For a first visit, the practical order is the one Tasting Table itself flagged: samosa chaat to start, paneer makhani for the table, and a regional main you do not usually see — the fish moilee with Malabar paratha or the kasundi fish steamed in banana leaf. The restaurant also lists vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options, and its adjacent sister cocktail bar, The Bar Beej, extends the evening next door.

A second Triangle location

The ranking is not Cheeni's only recent recognition. Durham Magazine's 2026 Best of Durham recognised Cheeni's Research Triangle Park location in three categories, according to coverage of the list. That second site, Cheeni Indian Food Emporium in Research Triangle Park, offers a casual lunch service and a preset, family-style dinner priced per person, while the downtown original remains dinner-only.

Diners can check hours and book through the restaurant's own site. Downtown hours are Sunday to Thursday 5-9 p.m. and Friday and Saturday 4-10 p.m., and the restaurant says walk-ins are available but reservations are highly encouraged, especially for larger parties, families with children and busy weekend evenings.

Why it matters for the Triangle

The Triangle has one of North Carolina's largest South Asian communities, concentrated around Morrisville, Cary and Research Triangle Park, and its Indian restaurants have long competed on regional depth rather than a single house style. A national list placing a homestyle, mother-and-daughter Durham kitchen at the top of the state is a marker of how far that scene has come — and a useful shortlist entry for diaspora readers deciding where to take visitors who want Indian food beyond butter chicken.
